description: Windows Firewall service, configuration, rule, and filtering events.

source.note: Firewall rule-change auditing must be enabled ('Audit Filtering Platform Policy Change').

4946.headline: A rule was added to the firewall exception list
4946.plain_english: A new firewall exception was added — a new hole was opened. If you didn't request this, someone may be opening access for an attacker.
4946.technical_description: Security event 4946: a rule was added to the Windows Firewall exception list. Records the rule and who changed it.

where.Computer: Machine where the change was recorded

4946.why_it_matters: Firewall exceptions expose services to the network — opening them is a common attack step.
normal_when: Documented rule for a new application
suspicious_when: Rule opens RDP, SMB, or another remote-access service to the internet
Rule created by an unexpected account or process
what_to_do: Inspect the rule (ports, protocol, profiles, source)
If unauthorized: revert and start IR

severity.high: Rule exposing RDP/SMB/WinRM broadly, or change off-hours

4946.important_note: Review the rule scope (interface, profile, source) — a rule can be harmless or catastrophic.

4948.headline: A firewall exception was deleted
4948.plain_english: A firewall exception was removed. This can be routine cleanup or an attempt to break expected access.
4948.technical_description: Security event 4948: a rule was deleted from the Windows Firewall exception list.

where.Computer: Machine where the change was recorded

4948.why_it_matters: Removing rules can disrupt expected access or break security monitoring.
normal_when: Documented cleanup of an obsolete rule
suspicious_when: Removing rules protecting a critical service
what_to_do: Check whether the removal breaks expected access

severity.high: Deletion of a protective rule or mass deletion

4948.important_note: Rule deletion is a common tactic to open access to a system by removing protections.

4956.headline: The active firewall profile changed
4956.plain_english: Windows Firewall switched which profile is active (Domain, Private, Public). Different profiles have different rules, so switching can change exposure.
4956.technical_description: Security event 4956: Windows Firewall changed the active profile.

where.Computer: Machine where the change was recorded

4956.why_it_matters: Profile changes can reduce firewall protection if the machine becomes less trusted.
normal_when: Network environment change (laptop moved from office to home)
suspicious_when: Switch to a less-restrictive profile that exposes services
what_to_do: Confirm the change corresponds to a real network change
Review rules in the new profile
4956.important_note: Profile changes are usually benign but can be abused.

5024.headline: The Windows Firewall service started
5024.plain_english: The Windows Firewall service started. This is normal at boot — but if the firewall had been stopped, this event can indicate it was restarted after tampering.
5024.technical_description: Security event 5024: Windows Firewall service started successfully.
5024.why_it_matters: Unusual timing can be a clue to tampering.

5033.headline: The Windows Firewall driver started
5033.plain_english: The firewall's kernel driver started. Normal at boot.
5033.technical_description: Security event 5033: Windows Firewall driver started successfully.

5059.headline: A key-file operation occurred
5059.plain_english: The firewall performed an operation on a key file (used to securely store configuration). Routine during firewall configuration changes.
5059.technical_description: Security event 5059: key file operation (firewall key store).
5059.why_it_matters: Key file manipulation can be part of tampering with the firewall configuration.

implementation_notes.verified_field: Only display a plain-English explanation when `verified` is true.
